data.title: US stocks bounce back; Nvidia shares shoot up 31% as Jensen Huang returns as CEO
data.description:
US STOCKS surged on Monday (Nov 23), led by a big jump in the Nasdaq as Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares after last week’s rout.

Nvidia’s shares shot up as much as 36.6 per cent after the board returned Huang. He had resigned from the company on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

US President Donald Trump said he secured a deal with Nvidia’s board to bring back Huang as CEO. Nvidia is widely seen as a cornerstone of the AI trade.

The news helped Wall Street recover from last week’s sharp selloff. On Friday, the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections as worries mounted about the AI trade.

The Nasdaq-100 added more than US$2 trillion in market value on Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 had their biggest daily gains since the market surged after Trump paused his “Liberation Day” tariff package in April 2025.

“The thought had been, and it’s being borne out today, that Jensen Huang is uniquely important to Nvidia and to the AI trade,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments.

Still, he said, “you have one issue that is resolved - and it’s a biggie - but you still have to see how the rest of things play out.”

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,447.98 points, or 3.01 per cent, to 49,595.31, the S&P 500 rose 326.78 points, or 4.73 per cent, to 7,237.17 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1,471.83 points, or 6.51 per cent, to 24,089.56.

Before Monday, the Nasdaq had come close to entering a bear market as investors worried about the heavy borrowing underpinning AI investment and questioned whether the sector could deliver sufficient returns.

Fears of political scrutiny also mounted after Democrats swept the US midterm elections.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index and S&P 500 information technology sector both were sharply higher on Monday, along with megacap stocks such as Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet.

Also climbing were neocloud and data-center companies, which had come under sharp selling pressure following Huang’s abrupt exit. Other sectors also rose, with energy being the only group in negative territory.

“We don’t think the rebound has run its course, and at these levels, it’s not too late to gradually add back technology exposure,” said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Ahead this week is Wednesday’s personal consumption expenditures report, which could give clues about the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy outlook. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: OCBC, Keppel, Starhub, Manulife US Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Tuesday (Nov 24):

OCBC : The bank has appointed Ang Eng Siong, the current CEO of OCBC China, as its new head of global corporate banking from Jan 1, 2027. The appointment comes as the bank reorganises its wholesale banking business into three divisions. Under the new structure, Ang will lead what OCBC calls “GWB 1”, focusing on scaling the large corporate segment in its core markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Greater China – as well as its overseas branches. Shares of OCBC closed 0.5 per cent or S$0.13 lower at S$26.41 on Monday, before the announcement.

Keppel , Starhub : StarHub announced that it will be acquiring Keppel’s M1 for S$1.1 billion. The deal is expected to close by the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval from the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA). StarHub also said that it has exercised its call option to acquire the Singapore operations of mobile virtual network operator Circles Life. Shares of Keppel closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent lower at S$8.83 on Monday, while shares of StarHub closed S$0.01 or 1 per cent lower at S$1.01, before the announcement was made.

Manulife US Real estate investment trust (Reit) : The trust manager said that it has negotiated a proposed agreement with its lenders that would allow it to exit a three-year debt restructuring and resume distributions to unitholders. The agreement is subject to unitholders’ passing resolutions at a Dec 15 extraordinary general meeting. Under the agreement, lenders would waive certain conditions under the Reit’s 2023 master restructuring agreement, and extend loans by about 12 to 18 months, excluding the sponsor-lender loan. Units of the trust ended flat at US$0.031 before the announcement.

data.title: Nvidia’s board was no match for Trump or Jensen Huang’s backers
data.description:
NVIDIA’S board already faced criticism for lacking the gravitas required to oversee the AI chip powerhouse – and that was before President Donald Trump chose to moonlight as a director.

“The board decided to do what we wanted to do,” Trump told CNBC on Monday after Nvidia announced it had reinstated chief executive officer Jensen Huang, just 11 days after he resigned following revelations of his affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a direct report.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it.” 

Trump even dialled into an Nvidia board meeting to argue for Huang’s return, according to Semafor, citing people familiar with the matter whom it didn’t identify. Asked if Huang would have been put back in place without his intervention, Trump told CNBC, “I believe my intervention was very important.” 

The president’s central role in one of the most dramatic corporate comebacks of all time marks the latest example of how he’s spent his second term blowing past the norms that have traditionally governed relations between the Oval Office and titans of industry.

The saga also shows how the directors overseeing one of the world’s most valuable companies provided little counterweight to Huang and his powerful backers, which risks undermining corporate governance more broadly. 

Trump’s interventions can shape business as profoundly as any economic force, as evidenced by his willingness to make statements that shift markets and demand government stakes in public companies. And the business of AI – with its huge national-security and geopolitical implications – has received much of his attention of late. 

“This is very much of a piece with the Trump administration’s penchant for interfering directly with corporate management decisions,” said Ann Lipton, a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder. “There’s no question it’s part of the same playbook.”

That playbook, which Columbia University law professor Jeffrey Gordon calls “Presidentialism,” is particularly evident when powerful CEOs can forge close bonds with Trump, as Huang has done, and insulate themselves from a board’s oversight. 

Huang, 63, had made a public plea to the board to bring him back, a move that was supported by some employees and prominent Silicon Valley figures. But the board initially rejected his overture.

Trump quickly and repeatedly praised the CEO’s abilities, saying Huang had already learned his lesson. Over the weekend, the president intensified that support by saying he hoped Nvidia’s board would rehire Huang. 

The president hailed the CEO’s return in a Truth Social post on Monday, saying the board had made “the correct and proper decision.” 

“It does look like we have a board that is not being run by its own directors, but out of the hip pocket of the White House,” said John Coffee, a Columbia Law School professor who specialises in corporate governance issues. 

Trump’s courtship of corporate leaders will likely increase now that he faces a Democrat-controlled Congress, said presidential historian Tevi Troy. “Building relationships with CEOs and making deals with them is something a president can do unilaterally, no Congress required,” he said.

Nvidia’s board said on Monday it decided to bring Huang back after it “received input from senior levels of the United States government.”

The surprise move to reinstate Huang was done without consulting the company’s senior leaders, who were informed of the plan at the last minute, according to people familiar with what happened. 

The board added that Huang’s reinstatement “poses no security risk” – an admission that raises questions about whether its probe into a possible Chinese foreign-intelligence campaign targeting Huang will be thorough enough. 

“This doesn’t look like a serious attempt to take the ethical issues seriously,” said Alison Taylor, who teaches business ethics at New York University.

If the espionage probe does unearth findings that implicate Huang, it’s unclear whether the board would remove him again, said R.J. Bannister, chief operating officer at Farient Advisors, which works with companies on compensation and succession programs. “Or does the return mean that discussion is over?”

The board said it had “every confidence in Jensen” but failed to explain how it’s now satisfied with Huang’s credibility given he was not candid earlier about his romantic indiscretions, according to Lucian Bebchuk, who heads Harvard Law School’s Program on Corporate Governance. 

“The board of directors clearly faced substantial pressures to reinstate Jensen Huang,” Bebchuk said. “These pressures resulted from the sharp decline in stock price and the support for Huang expressed by the President.”

Trump was one of the many business and political leaders who saw Huang, who built Nvidia from a niche supplier of graphics cards into a business valued at more than US$5 trillion, as irreplaceable.

Huang also was one of the leading cheerleaders for AI itself, crisscrossing the globe to promote what he called a new industrial revolution.  

But the AI sector has been weighed down of late due to heavy spending on infrastructure and fears that the Democratic landslide in the US midterm elections could slow the buildout of data centres.

News of Huang’s return triggered a historic rally for Nvidia. The shares climbed as much as 37 per cent, the biggest intraday surge since December 2000, helping fuel a broader rebound in US stocks after last week’s selloff. Before Monday’s rebound, Nvidia had lost nearly half its value since reaching a record high in early October.

Shelly Palmer, an AI consultant whose clients include Alphabet’s Google, said the Trump administration might even want to have some sort of advisory role in Nvidia now that it has intervened.

This wouldn’t be unprecedented: Nippon Steel’s acquisition of US Steel last year reportedly included a provision giving Trump veto power over major strategic decisions. The federal government is also a large shareholder of Intel, and the White House previously cast that arrangement as a possible template for deals with other companies. 

Late last year, following lobbying from Huang, Trump decided to loosen chip controls and allow Nvidia to sell its H200 processor — now generations behind its latest chips — to China. 

Nvidia’s board will have to tread carefully going forward, according to a person familiar with company leadership, who said directors could find themselves vulnerable if Huang decides to retaliate.

That dynamic could complicate efforts to develop a succession plan or tackle the company’s broader governance issues, the person said.

In their view, the board has emerged from the episode significantly weakened: Huang has yet to fully reestablish his authority, but could do so once the investigations are resolved, leaving directors with even less leverage.

For now, the board is taking some steps to improve oversight. The company said Monday it will hire a new chief compliance officer, and the board recently formed a committee to oversee national security and export control matters. 

That’s not enough, experts said. The board had already failed to fulfill one of its primary responsibilities, which was to identify a successor to Huang.

Now, it’s abruptly decided there can be only one successor: Huang himself. “This is a terrible day for US corporate governance,” Gordon said. “The directors should resign as a matter of personal and moral integrity.” 

What the board needs, Columbia Law School’s Coffee said, is “someone who can’t be told that he’s a lap dog, or at least he hasn’t yet proven that he’s a lap dog.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: The end might be nigh. Here, have some Anthropic shares
data.description:
LATELY, has every dire noise made by someone very smart and very far away made you want to throw up your hands and say: “Well, what am I supposed to do about that?”

You’re not alone.

While people have been wringing hands over where advanced semiconductor chips are headed, some artificial intelligence models – despite or because of their lack of opposable thumbs – are advancing at a freakishly faster rate.

In a report released in early November, METR, an independent research firm, estimated that Anthropic’s models have been improving almost twice as fast on certain benchmark tests compared with their pace from a year ago.

Crucially, this acceleration cannot be explained by more computing power thrown at training models. Rather, the AI itself has been getting better at helping Anthropic improve its models.

The upshot is that the AI development curve could become steeper yet. Now, some experts in the AI community have drawn vivid and unsettling extrapolations from the study’s numbers.

For instance, the AI Futures Project – an outfit that previously forecasted the onset of artificial general intelligence – has pulled forward its own grim timeline by five months, citing METR’s findings as its biggest new piece of evidence.

The AI Futures Project now expects a superhuman AI researcher to emerge by 2027, with a 35 to 65 per cent chance of AI capable of automating all white-collar work before 2028.

“I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within three to 12 months,” wrote Eli Lifland, its co-founder, on X.

And in a talk at The Hinton Lectures 2026 earlier in November, OpenAI Foundation board member Paul Christiano said: “For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”

We have a limited set of possibilities here.

Some of the smartest people on this planet, with first-hand knowledge of AI, could be spectacularly wrong.

They could also be exaggerating the technology’s capabilities in service of relevance or funding.

Or they could just be right: modern-day Cassandras shouting into the noisy vortex of initial public offerings and extravagant valuation multiples.

Even if the doomsayers are wrong about the future trajectory of AI, humanity is already struggling with the technology in its present state.

Companies and organisations have been woefully unprepared for the recent surge in agentic AI attacks.

Meanwhile, the US has learnt the hard way that there are limits to how effectively it can keep hardware away from rivals.

And no government has truly confronted the fiscal and social overhaul required if AI causes mass unemployment.

The average person, powerless to influence AI policy or commercial roll-outs, has been valiantly acting as rationally as they can, under the shadow of an abstract catastrophe.

Right now, any rational response looks indistinguishable from sanguineness.

When Anthropic started trading on Nov 19, investors sent its shares 17 per cent above the IPO price, implicitly buying into a technology whose creators have warned could end us all.

This is both perverse and sensible. If fears about AI are overblown, investors will live to reap the fruit of this and future IPOs.

And if the Cassandras are actually right, everything will cease to matter, simply because everything has ceased.

data.title: SGX tech stocks rebound on Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Tech counters on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) rose in early trade on Tuesday (Nov 24), tracking gains in the US stock market following Jensen Huang’s return to chipmaker Nvidia.

As at 9.15 am, AEM was up 11.5 per cent at S$6.69; CSE Global rose 4.6 per cent to S$0.80; Frencken was up 5.8 per cent at S$1.65; and UMS advanced 8.2 per cent to S$1.72.

Overall, the benchmark Straits Times Index was also up 1.3 per cent at 5,016.86 as at 9.15 am.

The rebound in SGX’s tech counters comes a day after Nvidia reinstated Huang as CEO, nearly two weeks after revelations of extramarital affairs. One involved alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang.

Nvidia’s shares shot up as much as 36.6 per cent after Huang’s return. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 1,471.83 points or 6.5 per cent to 24,089.56.

Meanwhile, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,447.98 points or 3 per cent to 49,595.31, while the S&P 500 rose 326.78 points or 4.7 per cent to 7,237.17 overnight.

data.title: Japan’s factory activity expands in November: PMI
data.description:
[TOKYO] Japan’s manufacturing activity grew at a slightly faster in November as output and export orders picked up on semiconductor and electronics demand, a preliminary business survey showed on Tuesday (Nov 24).

The S&P Global Flash Japan Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index rose to 53.7 in November from 53.3 in October, a preliminary survey by S&P Global showed. The 50-mark separates growth from contraction.

A key sub-index for factory output grew and new orders rose at a solid pace helped by a sharp rise in export orders.

New export orders accelerated from October, thanks to robust demand, especially from other major Asian economies. This lifted new export business at the overall private sector at the fastest rate since January 2018.

Manufacturers were more optimistic than service providers about the business outlook, but confidence in both sectors weakened from October on worries about rising costs, labour shortages and concerns over a slowdown in consumer spending.

Price pressures remained strong across the private sector even as they eased. Input cost inflation slowed to an eight-month low, while output charge inflation weakened to its lowest since March, though both stayed historically sharp.

“Japan’s private sector continued to expand midway through the final quarter of the year, but momentum was lost amid a slowdown in service sector activity,” said Annabel Fiddes, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

“Uncertainty remains elevated as firms grapple with sharply rising costs and worries over a sustained slowdown in consumer spending.”

The services sector weakened, with the flash Japan services PMI slipping to 50.5 from 51.7.

The composite PMI, which combines manufacturing and services, eased to 51.5, a six-month low, from 52.1 in October. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: AI should help Singapore afford a better retirement
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore’s decision to raise its retirement and re-employment ages advances an important principle: Older people should have more choices over how they spend their later years.

Artificial intelligence offers an opportunity to give that principle greater economic substance.

From Jan 1, 2029, these ages will rise to 65 and 70 respectively, a year ahead of the previous timetable. The government is right to strengthen protection for older workers who wish to remain employed. Longer employment protection preserves the opportunity to earn.

On the flip side, if AI enables us to produce more for each working hour, it can also strengthen the resources supporting retirement. Singapore’s approach to supporting an ageing society provides a foundation for pursuing both ambitions.

Productivity increases choices

The statutory ages protect covered employees against retirement on account of age, and require re-employment offers for eligible workers, subject to the applicable conditions. They do not oblige everyone to work until 70.

Central Provident Fund payout eligibility remains 65 for members born in 1954 or later. This separation allows employment protection to improve, while preserving the age at which retirement income can begin.

It gives practical expression to the distinction between enabling longer careers and requiring them.

Singapore’s emphasis on productivity is particularly valuable here.

A ratio of working-age people to seniors describes the population’s age structure. The economic capacity to support retirement also depends on how much each working hour produces and what essential goods and services cost.

An economy with fewer workers can still become more prosperous if productivity rises sufficiently. In September 2025, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong explained that most of the Republic’s projected growth would have to come from productivity improvements as workforce growth slows.

AI could contribute by enabling output to grow faster than the labour needed to produce it. But that prospect remains conditional.

On Oct 20, the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s chief economist, Edward Robinson, cautioned that a decisive economy-wide productivity increase was not yet apparent.

His distinction between today’s AI investment and tomorrow’s possible efficiency gains supports a prudent sequence: preserve employment options, build productive capacity and allow durable gains to inform future commitments.

Sharing AI gains across generations

Realising those gains requires companies in Singapore to remain competitive as AI changes how business is done.

The value comes from using the tech to improve products, services and working methods. Investment in skills and organisational change helps turn adoption into lasting improvements in what enterprises can produce.

Where these improvements support higher wages, workers can accumulate more CPF savings during their careers. Where sustained growth broadens taxable incomes and profits, it can also strengthen the revenue base supporting public programmes.

Both depend on viable enterprises generating additional value after the costs of adopting and operating the tech.

The timing of the gains enabled by AI matters. Younger workers may have decades in which higher earnings can strengthen their retirement savings. Someone nearing retirement has less time to do so.

For a person who has left paid employment, higher wages elsewhere do not directly increase the CPF savings already accumulated. Sharing future growth across generations therefore involves different channels.

Singapore’s existing arrangements recognise this distinction. CPF links earnings during working life to resources in retirement. Workfare adds cash and CPF support for eligible lower-income workers.

Silver Support assists eligible seniors who had low incomes during their working years and now have fewer resources, taking account of lifetime wages, housing and family support.

These arrangements allow economic progress to benefit people at different stages of life. Higher wages can improve future retirement incomes through saving, while government-funded support enables eligible retirees to share in prosperity that arrives after their principal earning years.

This is an important strength when technological change creates opportunities that successive generations experience differently.

The October senior employment package reinforces this logic. Alongside higher statutory ages, the government accepted recommendations to enhance the Workfare Income Supplement and update the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme.

Employment opportunities, sustainable wage growth and retirement adequacy are being advanced together by the government. AI-enabled growth could give that approach greater financial scope over time.

If broad-based AI adoption generates a durable increase in public revenue, future Budgets could use part of that additional capacity to continue strengthening established retirement schemes.

Targeted CPF top-ups could help eligible people still building their savings, while enhanced Silver Support could share the gains with eligible seniors whose principal earning years are behind them.

The scope would depend on assessed needs, other public priorities and fiscal sustainability.

Singapore’s fiscal discipline gives this ambition credibility. Lasting commitments require lasting resources, assessed alongside other public needs. Stronger productive capacity would enlarge the choices available within that discipline.

This is how AI could strengthen the government’s established approach to sharing the fruits of growth across working lives and generations.

A dividend of time and money

Retirement security also depends on how productivity gains are distributed across sectors.

If AI raises wages elsewhere while care remains labour-intensive, providers may face higher staffing costs without a comparable increase in the number of people they can serve. Stronger nominal incomes could then buy less additional care than expected.

This gives AI adoption in domestic services particular social value. Reducing administrative work could release staff time for patients and help providers serve more people with existing resources.

Where such improvements contain costs or improve access, they strengthen retirement security through the purchasing power of incomes, as well as their cash value.

For those who remain employed, some productivity gains could support shorter hours. Where a business can sustain output and cover its tech costs with less labour time, employers and workers can consider sharing the gains through time, as well as pay.

The government’s planned Flexi-Load Programme would help employers meet the transitional costs of creating part-time or fractional roles.

Alongside that support for job redesign, productivity improvements could make reduced workloads easier to sustain. The opportunities will differ across industries and individual circumstances.

Some people will want to work well beyond conventional retirement ages. Others will stop because of health, caregiving responsibilities or personal preference.

A more productive economy can strengthen the financial security within which those decisions are made. Greater security would give more seniors the choice and freedom to work for fulfilment or enjoy retirement.

Higher retirement and re-employment ages protect the opportunity to continue contributing. Successful AI adoption could complement that protection by making a secure retirement easier to finance.

The common purpose is greater prosperity with greater control over our time: a fitting ambition for Singapore’s next stage of growth.

The writer, a law lecturer at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, is author of the monograph Legal Personhood in the Anthropocene. He is also an associate academic fellow at the National University of Singapore’s Asia-Pacific Centre for Environmental Law.

data.title: US blacklists Megaspeed chip firm linked to Nvidia scandal
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] The US Commerce Department on Monday added Singapore-based Megaspeed, the cloud company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, to its trade blacklist, following criticism from lawmakers and administration officials.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner which has been under investigation by US authorities since 2024 over whether it diverted AI chips to China, will now need approval from the US Commerce Department to obtain US exports, which is likely to be denied. "The Department of Commerce still needs to explain to Commerce why this took so long," Senator Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, said in a posting on X. Megaspeed gained the spotlight about two weeks ago after news broke that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. China has said the spy accusations are "groundless." After the news broke, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly complained that the Commerce Department had not yet placed the company on its Entity List. He also called out Nvidia. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" Bessent told CNBC's Squawk Box programme. Nvidia has said it recently formed an export control committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. Megaspeed did not immediately return a request for comment. A week ago, the company issued a statement saying it conducts legitimate and lawful business, including complying with US export controls. It also said Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed in August 2025. The US Justice Department and Commerce Department issued a joint statement last week saying they would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred." Democratic lawmakers this week opened a probe into what influence Nvidia was able to wield over the Commerce Department's investigation. Besides Megaspeed International Pte in Singapore, the Commerce Department on Monday added six other companies from Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to the Entity List. All had some link to Megaspeed, a Commerce official said. The blacklisting coincided with Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia after his resignation two weeks ago. The last time the Commerce Department placed any new entities on the list was October 2025. As Reuters exclusively reported in June, the US has held off adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the trade blacklist, as the Trump administration tried to avoid escalating tensions with Beijing.
